claims.text: Adding 1–2 atomic percent Hf to an RHEA will improve its high-temperature mechanical strength.
Adding 1–2 atomic percent Hf will limit the alloy's density increase.
Adding 1–2 atomic percent Hf will preserve room-temperature ductility.
Hf addition will form fine-scale Hf-rich precipitates.
Hf produces solid-solution strengthening because of its atomic-size mismatch with other alloying elements.
The Hf-rich phases will be thermally stable at elevated temperatures.
Thermally stable Hf-rich phases will impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures and thereby provide precipitation hardening.
Atomic-size-mismatch strengthening from Hf will enhance high-temperature strength without significantly increasing density.
At 1000–1200 °C under tensile or compressive loading, the Hf-modified alloy will have at least 10% greater yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The Hf-modified alloy will have no more than a 5% density increase relative to the baseline.
The Hf-modified alloy will show no significant degradation in room-temperature ductility relative to the baseline.
The proposed effects are expected to extend to RHEAs having similar base compositions and processing conditions.
The proposed effects may not extend to alloys with significantly different chemistries or microstructures.

contradictions.description: HfNbTaTiZr is offered as an example baseline 'without hafnium addition,' even though its formula already explicitly contains Hf; adding 1–2 at.% Hf to this baseline is therefore not an Hf-free-to-Hf-modified comparison.
